title: Dispatch: a third-warmest July, 429.12 ppm, and a melt season nobody is narrating

blocks.text: A short round, deliberately. This is where the record actually stands on 8 August 2026, taken from the producers' own files rather than from anyone's summary of them. It is short because the month is not over, one of the four monthly temperature institutions has not reported and one was unreachable from this machine. Where a number does not exist yet, that is said rather than filled in.
THE AIR: JULY IS IN, AND IT IS 429.12

NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, monthly mean CO2 at Mauna Loa for July 2026: 429.12 ppm, against 427.87 ppm in July 2025. Read directly from the co2_mm_mlo.txt data file on 2026-08-09. The de-seasonalised value for the month is 428.83 ppm. Our own series held 429.12 ppm at decimal year 2026.5417 before this check and NOAA has not revised it; May (432.34) and June (431.44) also match unchanged.

The year-on-year change in NOAA's de-seasonalised Mauna Loa trend, month by month through 2026: January +1.97, February +2.27, March +2.00, April +1.48, May +1.84, June +1.83, July +1.25 ppm. Computed by us from the NOAA file on 2026-08-09.

NOAA's globally averaged marine surface monthly mean, a different and slower product from the same laboratory, runs only to May 2026 (428.73 ppm). The single-site Mauna Loa series is two months ahead of the global one, and they are not the same quantity.

The boring reading of that +1.25 ppm, and the correct one for now: it is one month, at one site, in a series NOAA itself flags as preliminary for the most recent year pending recalibration of reference gases. Monthly growth rates are noisy by several tenths of a ppm and this is a single point below a wobbling line, not a turn in it. Anyone reading a slowdown into it should be asked to show the same claim on annual means, which is the comparable quantity.

Our reading, held loosely: the interesting thing about a slow July is the calendar it sits in. WMO announced a developing El Nino in June and now forecasts a strong one, and El Nino years are historically when the land sink weakens and the CO2 growth rate jumps - 2024's record 3.76 ppm was exactly that. If the growth rate is easing while El Nino strengthens, either the sink is behaving unusually or the response has not arrived yet. We expect the second and will say so if it turns out to be the first. Either way the test is the annual mean, in early 2027.

blocks.caption: Atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa, monthly mean, ppm (NOAA GML), now through July 2026 at 429.12 ppm. Zoom into the last decade and the sawtooth is the northern biosphere's growing season; the July point is on the falling limb, which is why it is below May's 432.34 ppm annual peak and not a decline.

blocks.text: THE ICE: MID-MELT, AND NOBODY IS WRITING IT UP

Arctic sea ice extent on 7 August 2026: 6.131 million square kilometres, read by us on 2026-08-09 from the NSIDC Sea Ice Index version 4 daily file. That is the 11th lowest 7 August in the 43 years of the record and 0.670 million square kilometres, or 9.9%, below the 1991-2020 median for that date. The season ran 9.103 million on 30 June to 6.526 million on 31 July. July's monthly mean, 7.714 million square kilometres, was the 6th lowest July in 39 complete Julys.

An instrument change sits inside that comparison. The daily file's source column names NSIDC-0051 (DMSP SSM/I and SSMIS) for every day up to 31 December 2024, and NSIDC-0803 AMSR2 files from 1 January 2025 onward, following the end of the DMSP feed. The 2026 numbers and the 1980s numbers are not from the same sensor.

NSIDC's Sea Ice Today service has been reduced since 15 October 2025 because of non-renewed funding. Discontinued: the monthly and mid-month analysis posts, the sea ice analysis tool, sea ice volume, and the extent spatial comparison tool. Persisting: daily Arctic and Antarctic images, the ChArctic interactive graph, links to the NOAA Sea Ice Index spreadsheets, reduced user support, and the annual maximum and minimum announcements in March and September. Verified on nsidc.org/sea-ice-today, 2026-08-09.

Our reading: the data kept flowing and the reading of it stopped. For twenty years the NSIDC monthly post was the thing that turned an extent number into a sentence a non-specialist could use - which seas were open, whether the pattern was wind or heat, how it compared. That interpretive layer is gone for this melt season, and the gap is being filled by individual scientists writing in their own time. A CSV that nobody explains is not the same public good as a CSV that somebody does, and this is the first Arctic minimum in a generation approaching without an institutional narrator.

The boring reading of the ice number itself: 11th lowest for the date is unremarkable inside the last fifteen years, and higher than 2024, 2025, 2019, 2020 and 2012 on the same day. The 9.9% deficit is measured against a 1991-2020 median that is itself already a warmed baseline, so it understates the change against the early record. And with an instrument switch in 2025, part of any small year-to-year difference could be the sensor. There is no record in this number. September is when the season is scored, not August.

blocks.caption: Arctic sea ice extent, September monthly mean, million square kilometres (NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4). The melt season under way now ends in the next point on this line, around mid to late September; the 2025 value was 4.75. Note the instrument change from DMSP passive microwave to AMSR2 at the start of 2025, near the right-hand end.

blocks.text: THE JULY BULLETIN: THE DATA IS UP BEFORE THE PAGE IS

The Copernicus Climate Change Service July 2026 bulletin is published on the C3S bulletin file server, read there on 2026-08-09. Global mean surface air temperature for July 2026: 16.8999°C absolute, which is 0.6711°C above the 1991-2020 July average of 16.2288°C and which C3S renders as 1.4711°C above 1850-1900. That makes July 2026 the third-warmest July in the ERA5 record, which begins in 1940, behind July 2023 (+1.5244°C) and July 2024 (+1.4790°C) and ahead of July 2025 (+1.2491°C).

The bulletin's own press-release graphic is titled 'Average June-July temperature for western Europe reaches record high': June and July 2026 averaged over western Europe, meaning land inside 11°W to 15°E and 37° to 55°N, came in at 2.79°C above the 1991-2020 June-July average. Europe as a whole in July alone was 20.4860°C, 0.6604°C above its 1991-2020 July mean, which is cooler than July 2024 (+1.4918°C) and July 2025 (+1.2979°C). The record is in the two-month western-Europe average, not in July on its own for the continent.

Sea ice from the same bulletin, on OSI SAF Sea Ice Index v3.0 against a 1991-2020 reference: Arctic July 2026 extent anomaly -0.8781 million square kilometres, or -9.57%, the sixth-lowest July in the 48-year record. Antarctic July 2026, -1.0445 million square kilometres, or -6.36%. The OSI SAF baseline July extent is 9.1713 million square kilometres.

A fact about the access route, and a correction we are recording rather than hiding. When we read climate.copernicus.eu on 2026-08-09, both the Climate Bulletins summary page and the press-releases index still showed 9 July 2026 and June 2026 as the latest item. This round was drafted saying the July bulletin was not out. It was: the data CSVs, the figures and the press-release PDF were all already sitting on the bulletin file server at sites.ecmwf.int/data/c3sci/bulletin/202607/. For C3S the file server is the primary and the web page is a lagging index of it, and we will check the file server first from now on.

NOAA NCEI has not published its July 2026 global climate report: the monthly report URL for 202607 returned HTTP 404 on 2026-08-09, and the Climate at a Glance global land-and-ocean July series runs only to 2025. NASA GISS could not be checked at all - data.giss.nasa.gov refused connections from this machine across repeated attempts on 2026-08-09, returning no HTTP status. That is a fault at our end of the wire or a rate limit, not evidence the dataset is down, and we are not reporting a GISTEMP July figure we did not read.

The boring reading of third-warmest, and the honest one: July 2026 sits 0.0079°C below July 2024 on ERA5's own numbers. That gap is far inside the uncertainty of a monthly global mean, so second and third are not distinguishable here and the ordinal is an artefact of printing four decimal places. What the number actually says is that the last four Julys are clustered near 1.5°C above 1850-1900 with no clear ordering among the top three, which is a duller and more useful statement than any ranking.

And the boring reading of the two missing datasets: it is a calendar, not a signal. Monthly reports come out on a schedule, this dispatch is dated inside the gap, and a round written on the 8th of a month will often be missing a producer's previous-month figure. We note it so the absence is legible as a date rather than as a finding.
THE FORECAST: A STRONG EL NINO

WMO press release, 31 July 2026: a strong El Nino is developing and is expected to strengthen during August to October 2026, dominating global climate patterns, with above-normal temperatures expected worldwide and a classic El Nino rainfall footprint. Multi-model ensemble forecasts from the leading global producing centres indicate seasonal-average sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding 2.9°C in the key monitoring regions. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole is also forecast, and tropical Atlantic sea surface temperatures are expected to stay above average. The statement rests on WMO's monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update; the full El Nino / La Nina Update is next due in early September 2026.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, in the same release: 'El Nino is one of the most closely monitored climate phenomena in the world. But forecasts in themselves do not prevent hazards, people do.'

Our reading, and it is a model result being reported as a model result: 2.9°C is a very large forecast Nino3.4 anomaly, above the 2015-16 and 2023-24 events, and it is a seasonal-mean ensemble forecast for a season that has not happened, not an observation. What it licenses is an expectation about 2027, not a claim about 2026: the global temperature response to El Nino lags the Pacific by roughly three to six months, so the heat this event delivers to the surface record lands mostly in next calendar year. The projection is worth publishing here only because it is checkable, and we will check it against the observed Nino3.4 index and against the annual means when they exist.
PUBLISHED THIS WEEK

World Weather Attribution, rapid study published 30 July 2026: 'Climate change increases likelihood of compounding drivers of severe wildfire conditions in France and Spain', covering fires of 22 to 23 July in Gironde and Landes and 13 to 28 July across Toledo, Avila, Madrid and Guadalajara, with roughly 115,000 hectares burned in France and 140,000 in Spain. For central Spain the fire-weather event is assessed as at least 20 times more likely than in a pre-industrial climate and 41.8% more intense than in a world 1.4°C cooler, with a return period of about 6 years now. For southwestern France, at least twice as likely, 45.8% more intense, return period about 20 years.

Nature, volume 656 issue 8126, 6 August 2026: 'Climate benefit and ecological cost trade-offs for ocean iron fertilization' (published online 29 July 2026, doi 10.1038/s41586-026-10795-y). Sixty simulated years of iron fertilization across ten ocean biomes yield net carbon dioxide removal of 1.1 to 5.3 ppm, with more than half re-emitted within decades after fertilization stops. The Southern Ocean is assessed as higher efficiency and lower ecological risk; the equatorial Pacific as higher efficiency and higher risk, expanding oxygen-minimum zones and reducing macrozooplankton biomass.

Our reading of the iron fertilization result, placed next to the top of this dispatch: the entire 60-year upper bound, 5.3 ppm, is about four years of the current Mauna Loa rise, and more than half of it comes back. That is not an argument against the research, which is exactly the kind of quantification a removal proposal needs before anyone deploys it. It is an argument for keeping removal and emissions on the same axis, which is what this project's chart is for.
WHAT THIS ROUND COULD NOT ESTABLISH

No cross-check on that July temperature. ERA5 is a reanalysis and the three independent surface datasets that would test it - GISTEMP, NOAAGlobalTemp and HadCRUT5 - have not published July, so the 1.4711°C stands on one product with no second opinion, which is the exact situation this project's record-independence rule exists to flag. No September Arctic minimum, because the melt season has six weeks left. No verdict on the CO2 growth rate, because a month is not a year. The next three checkable things, in order: NCEI's July report around 10 August, GISTEMP's July when the server will talk to us, and the Arctic minimum in the second half of September - the one number this melt season will still get an official announcement for.

knowledge: Fixed the project's current state against the producers' own files on 2026-08-09: Mauna Loa July 2026 confirmed unrevised at 429.12 ppm with the de-seasonalised year-on-year run computed month by month for 2026; ERA5 July 2026 at 16.8999°C absolute and 1.4711°C above 1850-1900, third-warmest July but within 0.008°C of second; Arctic extent on 7 August measured at 6.131 million square kilometres, 11th lowest for the date and 9.9% below the 1991-2020 median, with the DMSP to AMSR2 instrument switch located at 1 January 2025; the loss of NSIDC's interpretive Sea Ice Today posts recorded as a fact about the observing system rather than about the ice; and a route rule learned by being wrong first - the C3S bulletin file server carries the month before the C3S web pages announce it, so the file server is checked first.
